slides.title: Build and test an architectural quantity calculator
slides.subtitle: Meeting B · Spyder practice with types, units, formatting, comparisons, and boundary cases
slides.teaching: Students open the Week 02 student file and confirm the working directory before running any exercise cell.

outcomes.head: Inspect
outcomes.body: Use type(), the Console, and Variable Explorer to verify representation.

outcomes.head: Calculate
outcomes.body: Build unit-aware arithmetic with explicit precedence and conversion.

outcomes.head: Communicate
outcomes.body: Format outputs so value, precision, label, and unit remain visible.

outcomes.head: Test
outcomes.body: Use known, boundary, and invalid cases to audit the calculator and AI suggestions.

slides.teaching: Students mark the outcome that needs the most practice and revisit it at the exit check.

items: Inspect values and repair ambiguous names
Test boundaries and audit AI-generated code
slides.teaching: Explain that each activity produces visible evidence in code, output, or a short written interpretation. Point out the recurring rhythm: predict on paper, then run, then a studio cell.

slides.title: The handout advances from a value check to a defensible model

tiers.task: Compare 12, 12.0, and '12'; then calculate 12.0 m × 3.0 m.
Convert '8.5' and '5.2', calculate area, and test area_m2 >= 40.0.
Test opening ratios for 0, 81, 162, and 200 m² on an 18 m × 9 m facade.

slides.teaching: Point students to the matching easy, medium, and hard activity labels in the editable handout. Require the expected check before each run.

slides.title: Recall the vocabulary used in today's script
rows: a name referring to a value
code that evaluates to a value
a question returning True or False
slides.callout: Say each line in words before asking Spyder to run it.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3, L4, L7, and the operator lecture. Students point to one example in the handout for every term.

slides.title: Repeat one studio cycle for every exercise

steps.label: PREDICT
steps.head: Write the expected result
steps.body: Include value, type, unit, or expected error.

steps.label: RUN
steps.head: Execute one cell
steps.body: Use Ctrl+Enter and leave later cells untouched.

steps.label: INSPECT
steps.head: Read the evidence
steps.body: Check Console output and Variable Explorer state.

steps.label: EXPLAIN
steps.head: Interpret the result
steps.body: State what the result means and one limitation.

slides.teaching: Model the cycle once. Prediction must be recorded before execution. Today's blue PREDICT slides are the whole-class version of step 01.

slides.title: Start by confirming the file and environment
slides.code:
from pathlib import Path
import sys

print(Path.cwd())
print(sys.version.split()[0])
slides.explainHead: Do not debug the wrong problem
slides.explainBody: Recall from Week 1B: import loads a module (pathlib, sys) so its tools become available by name. A correct working folder and known interpreter prevent many file and package failures. Save the handout copy before editing.
slides.teaching: Students show the printed path to a partner before proceeding. This reuses the import pattern from Week 1B—students should name it, not relearn it.

slides.title: Studio 1: classify values before using them
slides.prompt: Predict five values and five Python types before running the cell.
steps: Annotate int, float, str, bool, and None examples.
Run and compare with type(value).
Find each object in Variable Explorer.
Write one valid and one invalid operation for two types.
slides.teaching: The goal is to connect type to possible operations, not merely copy class names.

slides.title: Names turn arithmetic into an architectural model
slides.code:
a = 12
b = 3.0
c = a * b
print(c)

# revise as:
wall_width_m = 12
wall_height_m = 3.0
wall_area_m2 = wall_width_m * wall_height_m
slides.explainBody: Only the second version communicates concept, unit, and result. Readability is part of correctness when another person must audit the model.
slides.teaching: Students explain why c = a * b cannot be evaluated architecturally even though it is executable.

slides.title: Every part of an assignment line is a decision

parts.label: The result name
parts.body: Names the concept and unit: square metres.

parts.label: Assignment
parts.body: The right side runs first; then the name is bound.

parts.label: First input
parts.body: 12.0 m, with the unit carried in the name.

parts.label: Multiplication
parts.body: Width × height models a rectangular wall.

slides.teaching: Same line and same values as the previous slide, so 36.0 is already known. Walk the numbered parts in order and ask what breaks if each one is wrong: a vague name, a missing unit, a swapped operator. Part 2 is the state rule from Week 2A—the right side is evaluated once, at that moment.

slides.title: Studio 2: repair ambiguous quantities
slides.prompt: Rename a short calculator without changing its numerical behavior.
steps: Identify the architectural meaning and unit of every input.
Rename each variable using snake_case.
Add one comment for a modeling assumption.
Verify that the result remains 36.0 m².
slides.teaching: Reject names that are merely longer but still ambiguous. Require the unit suffix for measured quantities.

slides.title: Operator order decides this result
slides.code:
# 100 m2 plate, three 20 m2 service zones
area_m2 = 100
zone_m2 = 20
zones = 3

print(area_m2 - zone_m2 * zones)
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: Python multiplies before it subtracts. Reading strictly left to right gives 240.
slides.teaching: Everyone writes a letter down before anyone speaks. Ask the 240 group to say their reading order aloud—that is the misreading the next slide repairs with parentheses. 40.0 assumes every calculation returns a decimal; both operands are int here, so the result is int. 'An error' assumes - and * cannot be mixed without parentheses.

slides.title: Parentheses can change the procedure
slides.explainBody: The first subtracts three groups of 20 from 100. The second subtracts first, then triples the remainder. Grouping changes the model, not just the appearance.
slides.teaching: Students have already committed on the previous slide. Now run both lines, and have each student write one sentence describing each procedure and estimate the result mentally.

slides.title: An assertion writes a known answer into the script
slides.definition: assert checks that a condition is True. If it is True the script simply continues. If it is False, Python stops at once with an AssertionError, so a wrong number cannot travel into the next calculation. Recall from Week 2A: this is the course's first correctness check, and today's calculator needs at least two of them.

example.head: assert wall_area_m2 == 36.0
example.body: 12 m by 3.0 m must give 36.0 m². Writing that known answer into the script means the next person to edit it finds out immediately if the edit broke the arithmetic. Note == asks a question; a single = would rebind the name instead. Change 36.0 to 40.0 and the script stops on this line instead of printing a wrong area.

slides.note: A passing assert prints nothing. Silence is the pass signal — a blank Console does not mean the line was skipped.
slides.teaching: Run one passing assert, then change 36.0 to 40.0 and run again so students watch the AssertionError stop the script mid-file. Stress that the assertion records an answer worked out by hand, before the code ran.

slides.title: Studio 3: expose the intended grouping
slides.prompt: Repair an area-plus-allowance expression whose parentheses are missing.
steps: Translate the calculation into words.
Predict the wrong and correct results.
Add parentheses that match the stated procedure.
Create one assertion with a known answer.
slides.teaching: Use a small value such as 100 m² and 10% so the known answer is obvious: 110 m².

slides.title: Unit conversion keeps source and result separate
slides.code:
length_ft = 25
feet_to_m = 0.3048
length_m = length_ft * feet_to_m

print(length_m)
print(7 < length_m < 8)
slides.explainBody: The original value remains available, the factor is named, the converted name carries the new unit, and a rough range check catches order-of-magnitude errors.
slides.teaching: Ask why overwriting length_ft with meters would damage provenance. Estimate first: 25 feet is a little over 7 metres.

slides.title: Studio 4: build a transparent conversion
slides.prompt: Convert a supplied dimension and defend the result.
steps: Estimate the converted range before calculation.
Use a named factor and preserve the source value.
Print the result with its new unit.
Add a Boolean plausibility check.
slides.teaching: Circulate for unit labels and estimates. A correct number with a missing unit is incomplete evidence.

slides.title: One f-string, two objects to track
slides.code:
area_m2 = 44.26
label = f'{area_m2:.1f} m²'

print(label)
print(area_m2)
slides.question: What does the last line print?
slides.why: Formatting builds a new string. The stored number is untouched: area_m2 is still 44.26.
slides.teaching: The first print shows 44.3 m², which makes 44.3 the tempting answer for the second. Have students open Variable Explorer afterwards and read both objects: area_m2 is still a float of 44.26, label is a separate str. Rounding for display never edits the source value.

slides.title: f-strings join calculation and explanation
slides.code:
room = 'Gallery'
area_m2 = 44.234
label = f'{room}: {area_m2:.1f} m²'

print(label)
slides.explainBody: The object remains a number until formatting. The label records room, rounded display, and unit. Do not mistake one decimal place for measurement accuracy.
slides.teaching: Students inspect area_m2 and label in Variable Explorer and compare their types.

slides.title: An f-string is a template with slots you fill

parts.label: The label
parts.body: The finished text: an f-string produces a str.

parts.label: The f prefix
parts.body: Without the f, braces print as characters.

parts.label: A value slot
parts.body: Insert whatever room refers to right here.

parts.label: Expression
parts.body: Any expression works; it is evaluated first.

parts.label: Format spec
parts.body: One decimal place. Display only, after the colon.

parts.label: Literal text
parts.body: Text outside braces is copied exactly as typed.

slides.teaching: Read the line left to right by number. Ask what each part is responsible for, then delete the f in Spyder and run again so students see the braces print literally. Part 4 is display only; part 5 is the unit that makes the label architectural evidence.

slides.title: Studio 5: format a room-schedule label
slides.prompt: Create one readable line from a room name, level, and calculated area.
steps: Keep calculated area as a float.
Use an f-string rather than repeated concatenation.
Choose and justify display precision.
Include the unit and inspect both objects' types.
slides.teaching: Ask whether different deliverables may justify different displayed precision while preserving the same underlying value.

slides.title: Text and a number meet at a + sign
slides.code:
# a count that arrived from a text field
count_text = '12'
extra_floors = 3

print(count_text + extra_floors)
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: Python never guesses a conversion: + joins two strings or adds two numbers, never one of each.
slides.teaching: Show the real message: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. Options A, B, and C are three different assumptions about who does the converting; the answer is that you do, with float() or int(). Contrast this loud failure with Studio 9, where '12' * 3 succeeds silently and returns '121212'.

slides.title: Convert text before arithmetic
slides.code:
length_text = '8.5'
width_text = '5.2'
length_m = float(length_text)
width_m = float(width_text)
area_m2 = length_m * width_m

print(area_m2)
slides.explainBody: Strings preserve the entered characters. float() creates numerical values that can be multiplied. Conversion can fail, so validation remains a separate responsibility.
slides.teaching: Show the error from float('eight') only after students predict it.

slides.title: Studio 6: convert, calculate, and reject bad input
slides.prompt: Turn two dimension strings into a tested area calculation.
steps: Convert both values explicitly.
Calculate and format area with units.
Try empty text, a word, zero, and a negative dimension.
State which cases should be rejected and why.
slides.teaching: Students need not implement try/except yet; they should document observed failures and desired policy.

slides.title: The room sits exactly on the threshold
slides.code:
# the room sits exactly at the programme minimum
area_m2 = 40.0
minimum_m2 = 40.0

print(area_m2 > minimum_m2)
print(area_m2 >= minimum_m2)
slides.question: What do the two lines print?
slides.why: > excludes the boundary value; >= includes it. 'At least 40' is a policy, so write >=.
slides.teaching: A boundary case is the exact value where a rule flips. Anywhere except 40.0 these two operators agree, which is why the boundary must be tested deliberately. Ask which operator matches 'a minimum of 40 m²' and who is accountable for that choice—Python has no default policy.

slides.title: A comparison converts a rule into Boolean evidence
slides.code:
area_m2 = 44.2
minimum_m2 = 40.0
meets_minimum = area_m2 >= minimum_m2

print(meets_minimum)
slides.explainBody: The comparison returns a Boolean. Week 3 will use that Boolean to control program behavior. Today, verify the rule and boundary carefully.
slides.teaching: Ask what should happen when area equals exactly 40.0 and why >= expresses that policy.

slides.title: Studio 7: translate a requirement into a test
slides.prompt: Represent a minimum-area requirement with a named Boolean.
steps: Write the requirement in plain language.
Choose the comparison operator deliberately.
Test below, equal to, and above the threshold.
Explain whether the threshold alone supports a design decision.
slides.teaching: Require explicit treatment of equality. The Boolean is evidence about one criterion, not an overall quality judgment.

slides.title: One division, four plausible answers
slides.code:
# 18.0 m by 9.0 m facade, 42.0 m2 of window
facade_area_m2 = 18.0 * 9.0
window_area_m2 = 42.0

print(window_area_m2 / facade_area_m2)
slides.question: What does this print?
slides.why: Division returns the whole float. Rounding and the % sign are display choices you must ask for.
slides.teaching: Every wrong option assumes Python presents the result for you: B assumes automatic rounding, C assumes division reports a percentage, D assumes a unit is attached. The stored ratio is dimensionless and unrounded; :.1% on the next slide multiplies by 100 and rounds for display only.

slides.title: The facade ratio combines the week's core ideas
slides.code:
facade_width_m = 18.0
facade_height_m = 9.0
window_area_m2 = 42.0
facade_area_m2 = facade_width_m * facade_height_m
opening_ratio = window_area_m2 / facade_area_m2

print(f'Opening ratio: {opening_ratio:.1%}')
slides.explainBody: Inputs carry units, arithmetic creates area, division cancels units into a ratio, and formatting presents a percentage. Every step can be predicted and tested.
slides.teaching: Students trace value, type, and unit after every assignment. The stored ratio is the number they just predicted; only the display changed.

slides.title: Studio 8: challenge the model at its boundaries
slides.prompt: Run no-opening, half-facade, full-facade, and excessive-opening cases.
steps: Predict 0%, 50%, 100%, and greater than 100%.
Verify all four results in the same script.
Add assertions for the three known valid cases.
Write a warning policy for invalid geometry.
slides.teaching: Students should identify that the formula can calculate an impossible geometry; validity requires an additional rule.

slides.title: Studio 9: audit AI-generated calculator code
slides.prompt: AI multiplies the string '12' by 3 and calls the result area.
steps: Predict the intermediate object and its type.
Repair conversion, names, units, and formatted output.
Add a known-answer assertion.
Record what you accepted, modified, and rejected.
slides.teaching: Expected repaired area is 36.0 m². The important insight is that the original multiplication succeeds while expressing the wrong operation: '12' * 3 returns the string '121212'. Compare it with the earlier + prediction, which failed loudly instead.

slides.title: Save a compact evidence package

steps.label: SCRIPT
steps.head: Complete .py file
steps.body: Runs from the top after a restart.

steps.label: RECORD
steps.head: AI-use note
steps.body: Explains accepted, modified, or rejected suggestions.

slides.teaching: Students confirm all four artifacts before the exit demonstration. At least two assertions are required.

slides.title: Exit check: explain one evidence chain
slides.prompt: Choose one calculator and narrate it without reading comments.
steps: Name every input and unit.
Explain every operator and conversion.
State one expected result and one boundary case.
Name one limitation outside the calculation.
slides.teaching: Cold-call two volunteers for concise explanations. This is preparation for code reviews later in the course.

slides.title: A calculator is credible only when its meaning survives
takeaways: Carry concept and unit in names.
Use formatting to communicate—not to manufacture accuracy.
Test known, boundary, and invalid cases.
slides.teaching: Students save, restart, run from the top, and submit the completed handout.
